problems.location: Concept 1: Situated Learning and Workplace Learning Ecologies / block 1
problems.lesson_text: While each model aims to prepare Priya for the same deliverable, they reflect fundamentally divergent theories of human learning.
problems.source_text: Same person, same project, same first deliverable. Different ecosystem. ... In Case C Case Aʼs course ... In Case C Case Bʼs platform
problems.reason: The slides treat Case C's ecosystem as one that includes Case A's course and Case B's platform, while the lesson frames the three cases as rival paradigms built on divergent theories of learning.

problems.location: Concept 1: Situated Learning and Workplace Learning Ecologies / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Abstract rule encoding and didactic memorization
problems.source_text: A well-designed three-day course before the project starts ... How much control she has
problems.reason: The slides only name the structural dimensions for discussion; the table's filled-in values (a 'well-designed' course recast as didactic memorization with static slide decks, agency rated Low/Moderate/High) are not in the source.

problems.location: Concept 2: The Spectrum of Visible and Invisible Artificial Intelligence / block 1
problems.lesson_text: As AI recedes into the invisible background, it reduces cognitive friction but often robs the learner of **metacognitive cues**, diminishes agency, and quietly enforces institutional assumptions without accountability.
problems.source_text: None of the nine below is good or bad on its own. A screen reader and a screening tool can both be the right call or the wrong one. What changes the outcome is whether someone chose it on purpose, and whether the person on the other end knew.
problems.reason: The Compass page says visibility itself is neither good nor bad, but this block casts visible AI as keeping oversight and invisible AI as robbing agency and accountability.

problems.location: Concept 2: The Spectrum of Visible and Invisible Artificial Intelligence / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Without audit protocols, these algorithmic classifications become self-fulfilling prophecies that limit learner access and institutional mobility.
problems.source_text: It can feel like being understood. It also means next year’s teacher meets the label before they meet the learner.
problems.reason: The source says the label reaches the teacher before the learner does, but the claim that sorting becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy limiting access and mobility is not in any source.

problems.location: Concept 4: Generative and Inferential Strategies for Conceptual Understanding / block 1
problems.lesson_text: rather than "feedback threshold models" (Kempton, 1986)
problems.source_text: two common but incompatible models for home heat control are the “valve model” and the “feedback model” (Kempton, 1986)
problems.reason: The quoted term credited to Kempton adds the word 'threshold' to the source's 'feedback model'.

problems.location: Concept 4: Generative and Inferential Strategies for Conceptual Understanding / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Outperformed text summarization when learning spatial/relational domains like molecular biology (Leopold & Leutner).
problems.source_text: Leopold and Leutner (2012) asked high school students who were studying a science text about water molecules, which contained descriptions of several spatial relations, to either draw diagrams, write a summary of the text, or to re-read the text
problems.reason: The study used a chemistry text about water molecules, not molecular biology.

problems.location: Concept 4: Generative and Inferential Strategies for Conceptual Understanding / block 2
problems.lesson_text: Tutors often learn more than tutees through the generative demand of preparation (Bargh & Schul; Roscoe & Chi).
problems.source_text: research on tutoring has shown that while students certainly learn by being tutored, the tutors themselves learn from the experience (see Roscoe and Chi, 2007)
problems.reason: The source says tutors also learn, and Bargh and Schul compared preparing to teach with studying for a test; it never says tutors learn more than tutees.

problems.location: Concept 4: Generative and Inferential Strategies for Conceptual Understanding / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Neural consolidation and inferential schemas develop exclusively through the effortful struggle of mapping, questioning, and resolving contradictions.
problems.source_text: The brain continues the work of encoding and consolidation during sleep and facilitates generalizations across learning episodes
problems.reason: The source says consolidation also happens during sleep (as the lesson's own Concept 3 says), so it does not come 'exclusively' from effortful struggle.

problems.location: Concept 5: Motivational Systems, Mindsets, and Self-Regulated Learning / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Automated behavior tracking (such as public green-yellow-red behavior charts or algorithmic proctoring systems) frequently prompts learners to infer that the institution's primary aim is behavioral control rather than learning.
problems.source_text: Why does a standard chart meant to help the teachers monitor, reward, and correct students’ behavior seem to undermine this boy’s enthusiasm for school? ... This example is a reminder that sometimes the materials and strategies that teachers intend to support learning can have the opposite effect for some students.
problems.reason: The source's green-yellow-red chart is a teacher-run scheme shown through one boy's letter as harming 'some students', not automated tracking that 'frequently' does this, and proctoring systems are not in the source.

problems.location: Exercise 1.2: Analyzing structural versus surface differences in situated workplace learning environments / block 3
problems.lesson_text: Maps six touchpoints: Recognizes formal (senior modeling), informal (peer tips), community (forum), relational (team interactions), work-based (project integration), and self-paced elements, showing distributed learning.
problems.source_text: Required formal ... Onboarding, certification, bootcamps ... Relational ... People leads, mentors, buddies, managers
problems.reason: The grading key labels senior consultants modeling the tool in meetings as the formal touchpoint, lists 'informal' (not one of the six) and expects a self-paced element, which contradicts the source's touchpoints and a situation that skipped formal training.

problems.location: Concept 6: Sociocultural Contexts, Learner Identity, and Asset-Based Design / block 4
problems.lesson_text: When AI systems quietly classify, track, or score learners using rigid, standardized language patterns or narrow rubrics, they risk codifying stereotype threat and institutionalizing opportunity gaps under the guise of objective analytics.

problems.reason: Stereotype threat was taught as anxiety triggered by identity cues, but the block never explains how an AI classification would produce it, so the link is asserted rather than reasoned.
